headline: Anthropic warns it may soon cross its own threshold for faster AI progress
dek: Anthropic's IPO filing warns it may imminently meet a threshold in its own Responsible Scaling Policy, as The New York Times sues Brave over scraping[S1][S3].
what_happened: Anthropic's new filing warns it may soon meet its own threshold for accelerated progress, though no current model crosses it[S1].
The New York Times and three other papers sued Brave, alleging it scraped their articles and sold access to AI companies[S3].
Gemini reads your Gmail to summarise and draft replies, and Google says it does not train its foundational AI models on personal emails[S4].

sections.title: Anthropic says it may soon reach its own threshold for self-accelerating AI
paragraphs: Anthropic added new warnings to the Risk Factors section of its revised S-1A filing on Monday[S1]. The filing says the company may imminently meet a threshold set in its own Responsible Scaling Policy[S1]. TechCrunch reads this as a warning that Anthropic is close to recursive self-improvement, or RSI[S1]. The same filing also updated the company's financials, showing revenue and expenses both rising[S1].

Anthropic says it uses AI in its own research and development[S1]. The filing warns this may cause its models' capabilities to advance faster than its ability to build matching safety, alignment and security measures[S1]. It also says the company has in the past not identified a significant acceleration in its rate of development until after it happened[S1]. Anthropic says it has not designated any of its current models as exceeding this threshold[S1]. The warning rests on internal estimates and expectations about future models, not current ones[S1].

RSI is the point where AI becomes good enough at training itself that progress speeds up sharply[S1]. Some people see it as a danger that could slip beyond human control[S1]. Others see it as a source of huge productivity and scientific discovery[S1]. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy is its plan to monitor and reduce these risks as that point approaches[S1].

card.hook: Anthropic tells investors its AI may soon speed up its own progress[S1].
points: The warning sits in the Risk Factors of Anthropic's revised S-1A filing[S1].
It says capabilities may advance faster than its safety, alignment and security measures[S1].
Anthropic says it has missed such jumps before, and no current model crosses the line[S1].
card.take: When the builder itself warns that safety may lag, the debate about AI speed stops being theory[S1].
card.ask: Should AI labs slow down when safety lags[S1]?
card.angle: The lab building frontier AI tells investors its AI may soon speed up its own progress faster than safety can follow.

desk.why: A giant AI lab warning investors its AI may soon accelerate itself; startling and widely discussed

sections.title: The New York Times sues Brave over AI scraping and paywall bypassing
paragraphs: The New York Times sued Brave, the company behind the privacy-focused Brave browser, on Monday[S3]. The suit alleges Brave scraped the paper's copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to AI companies[S3]. The Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit the same day[S3]. Both cases were brought in federal court in Manhattan[S3].

The suit says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it[S3]. According to the complaints, Brave sells AI companies paid access to content from that index[S2]. The customers named are Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere[S3]. The suits also target a Brave browser feature that lets users bypass paywalls[S3]. The publishers say Brave never asked their permission or paid them[S2].
The New York Times has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims[S3]. Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment[S3].

card.hook: The New York Times sues Brave, saying it sold scraped news to AI firms[S3].
points: The suit says Brave indexed more than 30 billion web pages with an unidentified crawler[S3].
Named customers include Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere[S3].
Three more papers filed a similar lawsuit the same day in Manhattan[S3].
card.take: The copyright fight is moving from AI labs to the companies that supply their data[S3].
card.ask: Should AI companies pay for the news they use[S3][S2]?
card.angle: The paywall fight reaches the companies that feed AI labs, and the named buyers include Anthropic and xAI.

desk.why: Big-name lawsuit with AI giants named as buyers, but the defendant Brave is less known

sections.title: What Gemini does with your Gmail, according to Google
paragraphs: Google has rolled out many Gemini features across Gmail this year, Engadget reports[S4]. Gemini can summarise recent emails, create to-do lists and draft replies[S4]. Many of these free features are switched on by default[S4]. That has raised concerns about whether putting Gemini in Gmail violates users' privacy[S4].

To do these tasks, Gemini needs access to the content of your emails[S4]. In a statement from April 2026, Google says it does not train its foundational AI models, including Gemini, on personal emails[S4]. Google says Gemini only accesses your inbox for isolated tasks such as summarising or drafting[S4]. It says Gemini processes your information to complete the request and does not hold onto it afterwards[S4]. Google's support page says the same safeguards Cover Chat, Calendar, Docs, Drive, Sheets and Slides[S4].

A large language model is the kind of AI system behind chatbots like Gemini[S4]. Many AI companies also face lawsuits accusing them of mass copyright infringement[S4]. That is why users ask whether their own emails could end up as training data[S4]. Engadget says turning off smart features can also switch off spelling and grammar checks[S4].

card.hook: Gemini can read your Gmail, and many of its features are on by default[S4].
points: Gemini summarises recent emails, creates to-do lists and drafts replies[S4].
Google says it does not train Gemini on your personal emails[S4].
Google says Gemini does not hold onto your data after each request[S4].
card.take: Open your Gmail settings and check which Gemini features are switched on[S4].
card.ask: Do you let AI read your work email[S4]?
card.angle: Gemini is already reading the inbox of anyone on Gmail, often by default; what Google says it does with that.

desk.why: Touches every Gmail user directly, with a clear check-your-settings angle

sections.title: An op-ed argues the SEC should block Anthropic's IPO
paragraphs: Anthropic filed the registration statement for its initial public offering last week, ahead of a planned November stock market debut[S5]. In an opinion piece, Matt Scherer argues the SEC should block the listing[S5]. Scherer is co-author of a report on protecting people and the economy if an AI bubble bursts[S5]. He says the company's finances look stronger on the surface than underneath[S5].

Scherer writes that Anthropic has $96 billion in cash reserves[S5]. He says its amended registration statement shows at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to five companies: Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google and Microsoft[S5]. He says footnotes reveal nearly $900 billion in spending commitments in total, most stretching into the 2030s[S5]. He notes the 2026 results have not been formally audited[S5]. He argues third-quarter results suggest revenue growth slowed over the summer[S5].

Scherer argues that spending commitments like these work like debts, because the payments are contractually required in future[S5]. His worry is that workers, retail investors and retirees could be left holding the bag[S5].

card.hook: A critic says Anthropic's $582 billion in commitments should stop its IPO[S5].
points: Anthropic plans a November stock market debut, the op-ed says[S5].
Matt Scherer counts $96 billion in cash against far larger spending commitments[S5].
He notes Anthropic's 2026 results have not been formally audited[S5].
card.take: This is one critic's reading of the filing, not a regulator's decision[S5].
card.ask: Would you buy shares in an AI lab[S5]?
card.angle: One critic reads Anthropic's IPO filing and sees giant bills; an opinion, not a ruling.

desk.why: One critic's opinion with big numbers; finance insiders care more than most viewers

sections.title: Anthropic steers Claude Code away from cloning existing video games
paragraphs: Anthropic has updated Claude Code's system prompt so the tool is not used to re-create existing video games, The Verge reports[S6]. Users can still use Claude Code to make their own games[S6]. Anthropic's Addy Osmani said the change applies to Claude Code on Opus 5.5[S6]. Tom's Hardware first reported the change, according to The Verge[S6].

Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot said to show two new sentences in the prompt[S6]. Osmani did not confirm that exact wording, but said Anthropic had added two sentences to the prompt[S6]. He said the aim is to steer Claude away from recreating someone else's specific game[S6]. He said using Claude to infringe intellectual property is against Anthropic's usage policy[S6]. Original games, genre games and games built from a user's own designs and assets are meant to keep working, he said[S6].

Retro gaming is being flooded with AI-made decompilations, recompilations and ports, The Verge reports[S6]. Osmani said Anthropic will keep adjusting the rule to strike the right balance[S6]. The Verge has asked whether other Claude system prompts will change too[S6].

card.hook: Anthropic told Claude Code to stop cloning existing video games[S6].
points: Anthropic added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5[S6].
Original games and games from your own designs are meant to keep working[S6].
Anthropic says using Claude to infringe intellectual property breaks its usage policy[S6].
card.take: If Claude refuses a game that is yours, Anthropic's Addy Osmani asked users to send it to him[S6].
card.ask: Should AI tools refuse to copy games[S6]?
card.angle: An AI lab quietly told its coding tool to refuse game clones; creators and gamers both have a stake.

desk.why: A clear AI refusal story, but mostly for developers and gamers

why_it_matters.text: Anthropic's warning sits in its IPO filing, not a blog post[S1]. The filing says safety, alignment and security work may not keep pace with its models' capabilities[S1]. It also says the company has missed such accelerations before, until after they happened[S1].

The Brave case targets a supplier of content to AI firms rather than an AI lab itself[S3]. The named customers include Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere[S3]. A win for the Publishers could change where AI companies get their fresh text[S3].

quote.text: dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI
quote.speaker: Anthropic
